title: Does the Equity Term Structure Respond to Monetary Policy Shocks?  - Liberty Street Economics
gist: Using the Giglio-Kelly-Kozak (2024) model applied to 1988-2020 data, NY Fed researchers find the US equity risk premium term structure is upward sloping (slightly negative at the shortest maturities, ~3.6 percent at fifteen years) and that BOTH hawkish and dovish FOMC surprises shift the whole risk premium curve up by roughly 25 basis points in parallel — statistically insignificant, but directionally symmetric. Only dovish (negative) surprises cut expected dividend growth, by over 50bp at the short end and 20bp at the long end, consistent with rate cuts signaling deteriorating growth. The practical read: monetary policy surprises move equity duration mainly through the growth leg, not through a differential repricing of long- vs short-dated cash flows.

themes.theme: Shape of the equity risk premium curve

insights.claim: The term structure of US equity risk premia is upward sloping, starting slightly negative at the shortest maturities and converging toward 3.6 percent at the fifteen-year horizon, based on Giglio, Kelly, and Kozak (2024) estimates averaged over 1988-2020.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Gives a hard anchor for what long-duration equity cash flows should be discounted at — near-dated equity strips carry almost no risk premium, so duration-heavy growth exposure needs ~3.6 percent excess compensation to be fairly priced.
insights.quote: the term structure is upward sloping, starting slightly negative for the shortest maturities and converging towards 3.6 percent at the fifteen-year horizon

insights.claim: Expected dividend growth rates net of the risk-free rate are essentially flat across maturities at around three percent, implying short-horizon growth expectations converge to the long-run rate rather than displaying a growth term premium.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Since the growth leg is flat, essentially all the slope in equity discount rates comes from the risk premium, so cross-maturity valuation dispersion is a risk-appetite story, not a growth story.
insights.quote: expected dividend growth rates are relatively stable at around three percent

insights.claim: The upward slope of the equity risk premium curve is interpreted as evidence that investors dislike long-duration cash flows more than short-duration ones because of greater exposure to risk and uncertainty, consistent with habit-formation and long-run-risk models.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Justifies a structural, not cyclical, valuation haircut on long-duration equities — a standing headwind for high-multiple growth names independent of the rate cycle.
insights.quote: investors dislike long-duration cash flows more than short-duration cash flows because of their greater exposure to risk and uncertainty

themes.theme: Symmetric, small risk-premium response to FOMC surprises

insights.claim: Dovish (negative) monetary policy surprises are associated with an average 25-basis-point increase in the equity risk premium, and the increase is uniform across maturities — a parallel upward shift in the level of the curve rather than a change in its slope.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Rate-cut surprises do not selectively cheapen long-duration equity; if you trade the cut, expect level repricing of the whole equity discount curve, not a duration rotation.
insights.quote: Negative surprises are associated with, on average, a 25-basis-point increase in the average risk premium. This effect is uniform across different maturities and indicates a parallel upward shift in the level of the risk premium.
insights.locator: Are Monetary Policy Shocks Good or Bad News?

insights.claim: Hawkish (positive) policy surprises produce risk premium movements similar to dovish surprises, suggesting rapid rate hikes also signal bad news about the economy — for example supply-side inflationary pressures.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Breaks the intuitive sign convention: equity risk compensation rises on surprises in either direction, so option structures paying off on FOMC-driven risk-premium expansion should be direction-agnostic, not directional.
insights.quote: we observe similar movements following positive monetary policy surprises, potentially suggesting that rapid rate hikes often signal similar bad news about the economy (for instance, supply side inflationary pressures)
insights.locator: Are Monetary Policy Shocks Good or Bad News?

insights.claim: The risk premium effects of both hawkish and dovish surprises are small in economic magnitude and statistically insignificant, which the authors attribute to the fact that at most FOMC meetings the surprises themselves are very small.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: A caution against overfitting equity strategy to typical FOMC days — the signal only plausibly matters in the tail of large surprises, so size the trade to the surprise, not to the meeting calendar.
insights.quote: The effects of both negative and positive surprises are not very large in economic magnitude and are statistically insignificant, but this may be explained by the fact that, at most FOMC meetings, these surprises are very small.
insights.locator: Are Monetary Policy Shocks Good or Bad News?

insights.claim: The paper's headline conclusion is that only large interest rate shocks induce a parallel increase in the level of the equity risk premium, meaning the effect is concentrated in tail events rather than in routine policy news.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Frame FOMC equity risk as convex: negligible on ordinary meetings, level-shifting on outliers — an argument for cheap tail hedges around high-uncertainty meetings rather than persistent FOMC-day positioning.
insights.quote: Our findings suggest that large interest rate shocks induce a parallel increase in the level of equity risk premium.

insights.claim: Expected dividend growth rates co-move only with dovish surprises, dropping over 50 basis points at the shortest maturities and 20 basis points at the longest maturities after negative monetary policy surprises.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: The damage from a dovish shock lands disproportionately on near-term cash flows — bad for high-payout, short-duration and cyclical dividend names, relatively less bad for long-duration compounders.
insights.quote: There is an over 50-basis-point drop for the shortest maturities and a 20-basis-point decrease for the longest maturities.
insights.locator: Lastly, expected dividend growth rates appear

insights.claim: Hawkish surprises do not lower expected dividend growth, which the authors read as evidence that rate hikes often reflect strong demand conditions or inflationary pressures that do not necessarily reduce nominal economic growth.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Supports fading the reflexive 'hikes kill earnings' trade — nominal cash flow expectations survive hawkish surprises, so the equity hit is a discount-rate event, not an earnings event.
insights.quote: This may suggest that interest rate hikes often reflect strong demand conditions or inflationary pressures, which do not necessarily reduce nominal economic growth.
insights.locator: Lastly, expected dividend growth rates appear

insights.claim: The monetary policy information channel — the idea that surprise rate cuts leak the Fed's private information about a weakening economy — receives partial support: dovish surprises depress growth expectations, but the risk-premium response fails to distinguish hawkish from dovish news.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Use the information channel to interpret the growth leg of equity repricing, but do not rely on it to predict the sign of the risk-premium leg around FOMC.
insights.quote: sudden cuts in interest rates signal private information about a weakening economy, which should in turn affect both risk premia and expected dividend growth rates
insights.locator: Are Monetary Policy Shocks Good or Bad News?

insights.claim: Monetary policy surprises are constructed via high-frequency identification — price changes in interest-rate-linked futures within a narrow window around FOMC announcements — with positive values denoting hawkish surprises and negative values dovish ones.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Defines the exact object being traded around: the surprise is relative to futures-implied expectations, so a cut that markets fully priced generates no shock and no expected equity repricing.
insights.quote: monetary policy surprises (MPS) are constructed by examining price changes in interest rate-linked futures contracts within a narrow window around FOMC announcements

insights.claim: The analysis uses the San Francisco Fed's Monetary Policy Surprise dataset built from Bauer and Swanson (2023), which extracts shocks from different-maturity Eurodollar futures and aggregates them into a monthly series running February 1988 to December 2023.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
entities: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco
insights.so_what: A publicly available, replicable shock series — anyone can rebuild this event-study overlay on their own equity factor book without proprietary data.

insights.claim: Because policy surprises are measured relative to prevailing interest rate expectations, the shock series does not align with broader economic cycles except at the onsets of business cycles, and averages close to zero over the sample with a slightly negative mean in NBER recessions.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Warns against using policy surprises as a recession indicator — they are orthogonal to the cycle except at turning points, which is exactly when their information content spikes.
insights.quote: Since the series represents surprises relative to prevailing interest rate expectations it does not necessarily align with broader economic cycles, except at the onsets of economic business cycles.

insights.claim: The Giglio, Kelly, and Kozak (2024) model estimates risk parameters by fitting the cross-sectional and time-series dynamics of stock market and fifty-one anomaly portfolio returns over 1973-2020, using principal components of anomaly returns and their valuation ratios as risk factors, and outputs monthly risk premia and dividend growth series across maturities.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: This is an equity term structure built without dividend strip data, so it extends to fifteen-year maturities where traded strips are illiquid — useful for pricing long-duration equity exposure that has no market benchmark.
insights.quote: The model estimates risk parameters by fitting the cross-sectional and time-series dynamics of stock market and fifty-one anomaly portfolio returns over the 1973-2020 period.

insights.claim: The empirical design is a coarse three-regime subsample split — positive MPS, negative MPS, and no FOMC meeting — comparing average term structures rather than running a dynamic event-study regression, and the overlapping estimation sample ends in 2020.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: A key caveat for anyone extrapolating: the results exclude the 2021-2023 inflation and hiking cycle entirely, precisely the period with the largest surprises the framework says should matter most.
insights.quote: we classify economic episodes into three subsamples: periods with positive MPS (hawkish surprises), negative MPS (dovish surprises), and no change (no FOMC meeting)
insights.locator: For simplicity, we classify economic episodes

insights.claim: Equity risk premia and dividend growth expectations are the two fundamental inputs to present-value equity pricing but are difficult to disentangle from stock prices alone, which is why the customary assumption of a constant discount rate across maturities is rejected here in favor of a maturity-matched decomposition into a risk-free rate plus a maturity-specific risk premium.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: A DCF that uses one flat WACC across all years systematically misprices long-dated cash flows relative to this evidence — the correct curve is upward sloping by roughly 3.6 percentage points over fifteen years.
